models.label: DeepSeek V4 Flash Vision Exp
models.headline: Cheap eyes, blurry vision
models.one_liner: A sparse-MoE vision bolt-on to DeepSeek V4 Flash that is by far the cheapest multimodal option here, but whose own docs disclaim fine-grained OCR.
points: Sparse MoE, 284B total / 13B active, 1M context, up to 384K output tokens; vision added to V4-Flash 0731 with text performance held constant (OpenRouter, vLLM recipes).
DeepSeek claims its multimodal agent benchmarks put it 'close to Opus 4.8', but publishes no reproducible figures and no third party has replicated them (the-decoder, DeepSeek API docs).
Vendor guidance explicitly lists fine-grained OCR, small-object identification, GUI grounding and hallucination calibration as limited, and tells you to human-review legal and financial documents.

Hacker News testers were harsher than the marketing: images reportedly downsampled near 800x800 ('kills a lot of use cases'), a clock read as 5:10 instead of 8:09:25, landmarks 6/12 versus a rival's 11/12.
Structured output is the weak spot for extraction work: OpenRouter lists tools/tool_choice plus response_format for JSON, but with no JSON-schema enforcement, so adherence is prompt-luck.
Genuinely fast and cheap at $0.22/$0.66 with 87 tok/s and 1.17s P50 latency on OpenRouter, the best price-per-image-token in this comparison set.
Labelled experimental by DeepSeek; reviewers uniformly recommend feature-flagging it behind a verified fallback rather than making it a sole decision source.

models.label: Ox Alpha
models.price_note: Stealth model — price unlisted while cloaked, not free forever
models.headline: Anonymous, hyped, unproven
models.one_liner: A cloaked 1M-context reasoning model that topped one small coding benchmark, that community fingerprinting keeps pointing at Z.ai, and that nobody can independently verify.
points: Pricing is NA because the model is cloaked, not free: it appeared 20 Aug 2026 for a roughly one-week free preview on OpenRouter and OpenCode, expected to close around 27 Aug, after which terms are unknown.

Community fingerprinting points at a Chinese lab, most often a GLM-5.3 variant: token counts across English, German, Chinese, code and emoji reportedly matched GLM-5.3 plus a fixed 75-token offset, with a 60-string LocalLLaMA comparison agreeing. No lab has claimed it.

The headline result is thin: developer Ben Davis scored roughly 80% on DeepSWE over just 10 tasks, versus 65% for Fable and 52% for GPT-5.6 Sol. Critics note a bash-only harness and a sample far too small to trust.
Abacus.AI's Bindu Reddy ran her own eval and called it 'worse than last generation models', scoring 'alongside Kimi 2.6 which is 2 generations old', while conceding it is 'pure marketing genius'.
Consistently described as slow and over-deliberating: 23 tok/s throughput and 5.49s P50 latency on OpenRouter, with testers noting it 'spins a lot' before producing anything.

Structured output is unenforced: OpenRouter lists tools/tool_choice and response_format for JSON but no JSON-schema enforcement. One reported agent run logged 69 tool calls with a single error and no retry loops.

Serious blocker for confidential documents: under the stealth agreement the anonymous provider retains prompts and completions (it states they are not used for training), and you cannot audit who that provider is.

models.label: GLM-5.3
models.headline: Frontier coding, cyber baggage
models.one_liner: The same 743B base model as GLM-5.2 with far more post-training, which pulled it level with Kimi K3 at the top of open weights and simultaneously made it good enough at exploitation that Z.ai delayed the weights.
points: No new base model: Z.ai kept GLM-5.2's 743B base and attributes every gain to scaled post-training with more task environments and longer training runs.
Artificial Analysis independently scored it 60 on the Intelligence Index on 18 Aug 2026, up 7 from GLM-5.2, tying Kimi K3 and sitting three points behind Claude Opus 5 at 63.
Z.ai's own long-horizon coding jumps are dramatic: Terminal-Bench 3.0 from 4.6 to 28.3 and DeepSWE v1.1 from 46.2 to 66.9, though it still trails GPT-5.6 Sol and Fable 5 on the harder coding evals.

Cybersecurity is the story: CyberGym 77.2% to 84.5% (past Mythos 5's 83.8%) and ExploitBench 24.4% to 54.4%, with 2,436 real vulnerabilities found across 269 projects after expert review and deduplication.
Weights were held back roughly two weeks post-launch for safety hardening, so the 'open weights' claim was a promise at launch rather than a download.

Structured output is unenforced: OpenRouter lists tools/tool_choice and response_format for JSON with no JSON-schema enforcement, and reasoning cannot be disabled, which inflates cost and latency on simple extraction calls.
Slow for the price at $1.40/$4.40 with 34 tok/s and 3.12s P50 latency; Hacker News split between 'only just by a hair' behind frontier and 'is post-training magic just overfitting to benchmarks?'

models.label: Gemini 3.7 Flash
models.headline: Fast, capable, JSON-flaky
models.one_liner: Google's workhorse Flash tier made a real jump in agentic coding, but it shipped with a documented schema-constrained JSON regression that is exactly the failure mode a structured-extraction benchmark punishes.
points: Big generational move on Google's own numbers versus 3.6 Flash: DeepSWE v1.1 65.3% vs 49.0%, FrontierCode 1.1 43.6% vs 34.4%, AutomationBench 30.4% vs 17.0%, WebDev Arena Elo 1588 vs 1538.

There is a live structured-output regression: with responseMimeType application/json plus responseSchema, prompts containing many near-identical items emit a valid JSON prefix then loop an integer field's digits until maxOutputTokens.

The reporter measured roughly 33% incidence on synthetic payloads and up to 100% on production equivalents, burning 241 runaway calls and about $60 of unintended output tokens in three days; retries re-entered the loop and temperature did not help.
The same bug does not occur on gemini-3-flash-preview, so this is a 3.7-specific regression, and no Google fix is documented in the thread.

Related complaints: agents terminating with empty output after a tool call, MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL on large function-call arguments across the Flash family, and schema key order not preserved in the Python SDK.

Migration is real API work, not a model-name swap: the 'minimal' thinking level now returns a validation error, thinking_budget is replaced by thinking_level, and deprecated sampling and candidate-count fields must go.

Price is the catch. OpenRouter lists $0.375/$1.875, but Google's own announcement puts introductory pricing at $0.75/$3.75 through 31 Dec 2026 and standard pricing at $1.50/$7.50 from 1 Jan 2027, so budget for a steep increase.
Genuinely quick and broadly multimodal (text, images, video, PDF, audio in) at 253 tok/s and 1.53s P50, with a 1M context but only a 65,536-token completion cap.

models.label: Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B
models.headline: Open frontier, premium price
models.one_liner: Alibaba's first Max-class model released as open weights, near the top of independent intelligence rankings but priced and clocked like a laggard on hosted endpoints.
points: Sparse MoE with 2.4T total and 95B active parameters, 512 experts (10 routed plus 1 shared), pairing Gated DeltaNet linear attention with Gated Attention in a 23-block repeating pattern.
Artificial Analysis independently places it at 58 on the Intelligence Index, ranking it #2 of 107 models evaluated and well above the 27 median for comparable open-weight models.
Alibaba's own headline numbers are strong: GPQA Diamond 92.6, PaperBench 93.0 (leading), OSWorld 86.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1 86.6, trading blows with Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.6 Sol on agentic tests.
It supports real structured outputs via JSON schema in response_format plus tools/tool_choice, which puts it in the better half of this set for extraction reliability.

Verbosity is a documented cost: it burned 140M output tokens on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index against a 100M median, and Qwen models are pre-trained to reason so they ramble even with thinking off.
Expensive for open weights at $2.00/$6.00 versus Artificial Analysis medians of $0.30/$1.20, working out to $1.09 per Intelligence Index task.

Speed reports conflict sharply: Artificial Analysis measured 45.1 tok/s and 2.54s TTFT (both worse than median) while OpenRouter's best provider shows 167 tok/s and 0.99s, so throughput is provider-dependent and worth testing yourself.
Long-standing caution from developers: Qwen's benchmark-to-real-world correlation has been inconsistent across past releases, so treat the vendor table as an upper bound.

models.label: DeepSeek V4 Pro (0813)
models.headline: Strong claims, thin proof
models.one_liner: DeepSeek's 1.6T flagship went GA with no announcement and a scorecard that would put it near frontier, except almost none of it has been independently reproduced.
points: 1.6T total parameters with roughly 49B active, pretrained on over 32T tokens, 1M context and up to ~393K output tokens, including a DSpark speculative-decoding module for faster inference.
Shipped with no blog post, changelog entry or press release on 12 Aug 2026, which is on-brand for DeepSeek but leaves reviewers working from third-party tables.

Vendor agentic numbers are aggressive: Terminal Bench 2.1 87.9 (vs 85.0 for Opus 4.8), CyberGym 83.3, AutomationBench Public 31.8, DeepSWE 62.7, NL2Repo 61.5, plus SWE-bench Verified 96.40% at roughly 1/36th the cost per test.
None of it is reproducible: the agentic harness was never released, and reviewers flag every headline figure as vendor- or analyst-reported.
The one independent read is Artificial Analysis at 53 on its Intelligence Index, up from 45 for April's V4 Pro, against Claude Opus 5 at 63.
No vision at all, and DeepSeek has signalled vision is not on the V4 Pro roadmap; this is the single most common complaint on Hacker News and r/LocalLLaMA.
Good structured-output surface for extraction: OpenRouter lists tools/tool_choice and genuine structured outputs via JSON schema in response_format, unlike DeepSeek's own Flash Vision variant.

Pricing is unstable and provider-dependent. DeepSeek's first-party API lists $0.435 input (cache miss) and $0.87 output with an unquantified increase announced, while OpenRouter routing sits materially higher. Developers on HN have already reacted with 'DS is dead to me after the pricing changes.'
Fast where it counts for batch extraction: 107 tok/s and 0.69s P50 latency across OpenRouter providers.

models.label: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning
models.headline: Blazing, cheap, shallow
models.one_liner: A 3B-active hybrid Mamba-MoE built to be the fastest hands on a keyboard rather than the smartest head in the room, and priced accordingly.
points: Hybrid Mamba-2 plus MoE architecture with roughly 31.6B total and 3.6B active parameters, released under the permissive OpenMDW-1.1 licence in both BF16 and NVFP4 checkpoints.
Cheapest and fastest model in this set by a wide margin: $0.08/$0.20 with 413 tok/s and 0.16s P50 latency on OpenRouter; Artificial Analysis clocked nearly 670 tok/s on a pre-release NVFP4 endpoint.
The tradeoff is explicit. Artificial Analysis scores it 24 on the Intelligence Index (a +9 jump over Nemotron 3 Nano's 15) but well behind Qwen3.6 35B at 32; Terminal-Bench v2.1 sits at 24%.
NVIDIA's own figures are better on knowledge-shaped tasks than agentic ones: MMLU Pro 81.94, GPQA Diamond 75.44, SWE-bench Verified 51.56, PinchBench 85.37 for the BF16 checkpoint.

It supports tools/tool_choice and true structured outputs via JSON schema in response_format, with reasoning toggled on or off through the chat template, and r/LocalLLaMA impressions describe 'clean tool calling' (impressions only, no independent table exists).

Best framed as an execution engine beneath a smarter orchestrator: formatting results, calling tools and grinding through repetitive volume, not the hardest single-pass reasoning or nuanced long-form writing.

Context claims conflict. OpenRouter serves 262K, while NVIDIA's model card claims up to 1M but concedes 256K is the practical ceiling on a single H100, with the full window needing 8xH100 or Blackwell.

Verbosity reports conflict too: one review says it emitted 100M tokens on the Intelligence Index against a 45M median, while Artificial Analysis's own launch note says per-task output tokens were similar to its predecessor.

models.label: Muse Spark 1.2
models.headline: Reliable runner-up, sluggish
models.one_liner: Meta's closed-weights coding model finishes a consistent second to Claude Opus 5 on Meta's own benchmarks, with the best structured-output surface here and the worst first-token latency.
points: A coding-focused point release of 1.1, co-trained with Meta's Muse Code agent on rejection-sampled harness trajectories plus a self-improvement loop where 1.1 generated and graded its successor's training environments.
Second place on all three of Meta's headline benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.1 82.9% vs Opus 5's 86.7%, DeepSWE v1.1 59.3% vs 65.0%, and Meta's internal coding benchmark 70.6% vs 79.4%.
Artificial Analysis independently scores it 54 on the Intelligence Index, up 3 from 1.1 and 11 from 1.0, effectively tied with Grok 4.5 but behind Opus 5, Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol and Kimi K3.

Those 3 points cost real money: input tokens rose about 53% and output about 36% versus 1.1, pushing cost per Intelligence Index task from $0.29 to $0.40. SciCode fell 2 points and Humanity's Last Exam fell 1.

Best-documented structured-output support in this set: genuine JSON-schema structured outputs in response_format, tools/tool_choice, parallel function calling and configurable reasoning effort. Tool-use benchmarks are still modest though, at 27% on Artificial Analysis's tau-3-Banking.

Hallucination profile is worth knowing for extraction: Artificial Analysis's AA-Omniscience puts it at 22 with a 28% hallucination rate and 67% attempt rate, with accuracy slipping from 41% to 38% as abstention rose.
Slowest to first token here by a distance: 9.50s P50 on OpenRouter at 84 tok/s, with 97.96% three-day availability, the weakest in this comparison.
Weights stayed closed, which the community forgave least: Alexandr Wang called Muse Spark 'not suitable for open sourcing' in May, then promised open weights on 10 Aug.
The cheap $0.10/$0.20 Contributor tier buys its 12-21x discount with permission to train on your data, which rules it out for confidential contracts.
